notable_claims: An informal survey was conducted regarding harassment on the Net.
classification.summary: This item is a repost of a summary regarding an informal survey on harassment occurring on the network. It highlights early community efforts to document and analyze social misconduct in digital academic and research environments.
classification.title: SUMMARY: Harassment on the Net survey

identity.subject: SUMMARY: Harassment on the Net survey

notable_claims: Some respondents expressed concern that addressing net harassment could lead to restrictions on the freedom of the Net.
A portion of survey respondents believed e-harassment is more easily ignored than phone or snail-mail.
classification.summary: Mike Holderness presents the results of a survey regarding sexual harassment on the internet, which was published in the Times Higher Education Supplement. The data tracks reports of direct mailbox harassment and chat-based abuse across various domains, including .edu and .ac.uk. The post highlights a tension between addressing online harassment and the risk of introducing restrictions on the freedom of the Net.
classification.title: SUMMARY: Harassment on the Net survey

notable_claims: The conference aimed to define ownership, rules, and access for the 'Information Superhighway'.
Cryptography was identified as a primary point of debate regarding government control versus digital privacy.
classification.summary: This is a detailed program announcement for the fourth Conference on Computers, Freedom and Privacy (CFP '94) held in Chicago. The conference focused on 'Cyberspace Superhighways: Access, Ethics and Control,' featuring tutorials and panels on cryptography, data protection, and the National Information Infrastructure. It brought together academic, legal, and technical experts to discuss the intersection of emerging network technology and civil liberties.

notable_claims: Newsgroup disclaimers can be used as a tool to prevent censorship of users.
Computer forums should be treated by university administrations like other types of forums.
classification.summary: A system administrator argues that the use of newsgroup disclaimers protects users from censorship. The author suggests these disclaimers help university administrations view computer forums as equivalent to other traditional public forums.
classification.title: Re: disclaimers

notable_claims: Disclaimers serve as protection against users who email system administrators to complain about other users' posts.
Some university administrations can be convinced to treat online forums as areas for free expression.
classification.summary: Wes Morgan argues that disclaimers are necessary to protect users from administrative retaliation when third parties report offensive content to university officials. He shares an example where his sports-related posts led to a complaint sent to the root administrator accusing the university of teaching racism. Morgan notes he successfully convinced his administration to treat computer-mediated communication as a forum for free expression.
classification.title: Re: disclaimers

notable_claims: A hypertext index of civil liberties netnews articles was available on the World-Wide Web in early 1994.
classification.summary: The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) shared a pointer to the Civil Liberties Index (CLI). This tool provided a hypertext index of netnews articles concerning civil liberties, accessible via early web browsers like Mosaic and Lynx.
classification.title: CLI: a hypertext index to "newsy" civil liberties articles

identity.subject: CLI: a hypertext index to "newsy" civil liberties articles

notable_claims: Distributing an index of articles instead of full text is a method to avoid violating ClariNet's copyright.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie announces the Civil Liberty Index (CLI), a tool designed to help users find news articles related to civil liberties without violating copyright. To avoid copyright issues with ClariNet's UPI service, the CLI provides an index of articles rather than the full text, allowing users to retrieve content from their own local machines. The index was made available via the World Wide Web (using Mosaic and Lynx), a mailing list, Gopher, and FTP.
classification.title: CLI: a hypertext index to "newsy" civil liberties articles

notable_claims: Students at the University of Illinois could set up unofficial WWW pages.
classification.summary: The post highlights a positive instance of academic freedom regarding digital space. It notes that students at the University of Illinois were permitted to establish their own unofficial World-Wide Web pages.
classification.title: A (positive) example of student archives

notable_claims: Student-paid fees for workstations make it harder to claim misuse of state charity.
Lack of an official index prevents the university from being blamed for offensive student content.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie highlights the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign's policy allowing engineering students to host their own WWW pages. He argues that using personal disk quotas and student-paid fees reduces institutional liability and accusations of misusing state resources. The post suggests this decentralized model avoids the need for an official index, thereby distancing the university from offensive content.
classification.title: A (positive) example of student archives
